SLA or Nay?

The impact of selective licensing on rental market outcomes in Bristol

Authors
Affiliation

Levi John Wolf

University of Bristol

Alex Marsh

University of Bristol

Published

October 21, 2026

Abstract

The private rental sector is an important part of the society and economy of any nation. The sector plays a critical role in accommodating a substantial proportion of households, particularly in urban areas. In addition, it is a major source of speculative investment, both for individual and small-scale landlords and, increasingly, institutional investors. At the same time, particularly in countries with liberalised housing markets, the sector faces issues of quality, affordability and precarity. These characteristics drive intense interest in the contemporary structure and regulation of the private rental sector. As a consequence, regulation of the private rental sector is controversial. This paper examines one key regulatory tool used in England, discretionary licensing, which requires rental properties in certain areas or that fit certain characteristics to meet minimum quality standards. Research on private rental sector regulations beyond price controls is rare, particularly at local level. Hence, this paper seeks to build understanding about the specific short-run impacts of the adoption of discretionary licensing policies in Bristol from 2019 to 2024 using spatial causal inference techniques. We find no detectable impact on market clearing, while the rent premium for comparable properties just inside the licensing boundary narrowed after licensing was introduced, by roughly £5 to £30 per week (£20 to £120 per month) near the boundary, depending on the identification strategy. This suggests that private rental sector regulation targeting minimum quality standards, such as those guaranteeing minimum energy efficiency, gas and electric safety, and other quality checks, need not raise rents or slow lettings in the short run, contrary to concerns that compliance costs would be passed on to tenants.

Introduction

The private rental sector is a large and significant factor in many countries’ economies and societies. Rental markets define individuals’ lives, in some senses; they govern where most people in their 20s live, and increasingly they shape how and where people are able to work and start families. In the face of a global affordability crisis, many people are living much longer in private renting, whereas in previous eras they would have transitioned to other tenures, principally owner occupation. In addition, it is a major source of speculative investment, both for individual and small-scale landlords and, increasingly, institutional investors. At the same time, particularly in countries with liberalised housing markets, the sector faces issues of quality, affordability and precarity (Kemp 2025). Since the 1990s the market in England has been considered one of the most liberalised in the developed world, with tenants typically being issued with six month tenancies and landlords allowed to evict on a “no fault” basis with two months’ notice. This level of precarity places limits on the effectiveness of consumerist approaches to quality regulation: consumers are reluctant to assert rights to remedy poor quality if it means they could lose their home. As a consequence, the regulation of the private rental sector is a significant political issue. Most analyses of rent control policies suggest that price-based rent controls have, at best, mixed effectiveness when considered as a whole across the city (Kholodilin 2024), with their negative effects on overall supply and the quality of privately-rented properties being key concerns. However, there is less agreement in the economic and policy studies literature on the impact of non-price regulation, including minimum quality standards, on the rental market. In part this is because there has been very limited empirical evidence, beyond the specific submarket of short-term rentals (Marsh et al. 2023). The grey literature specifically focused on licensing in the UK finds relative short-term success in the adoption of quality and licensing standards (Building Research Establishment 2010; Ministry of Housing 2019), and the policy has been argued to have benefits beyond improving housing quality (Petersen et al. 2022). Yet, other political advocacy groups argue that such positive evaluations ignore potential long-term and secondary effects of regulation of the private rental sector. In particular, there is a concern that the additional costs, both monetary and non-monetary, associated with licensing, are unnecessary; they will be passed on to tenants in higher rents or create a bureaucratic burden that will result in landlords exiting the market. This will exacerbate problems of housing accessibility in already pressured local markets.

Many of the policy models in the United Kingdom target specific segments of the private rental sector, such as rental properties with more than 5 people that comprise at least two separate households, or properties that fall into specific urban wards. This latter kind of neighborhood-level regulation has not been studied extensively (O’Toole 2023), and the evidentiary requirements for understanding regulatory impacts or, in the realm of policy, for justifying their use legally tend to be quite challenging to satisfy fully (Marsh et al. 2023; Gibb and Marsh 2022).

This paper seeks to shed light on this issue through a unique adoption pattern of neighborhood housing quality regulation policies in Bristol, England. Bristol City Council has adopted private rental sector regulations, known as discretionary licensing policies, that apply to specific urban wards. These policies, as discussed below, have different impacts on different types of properties, and may generate localized externalities that distort local urban rental markets. This paper seeks to identify whether, specifically, covering most of central Bristol in discretionary licensing areas from 2019 to 2024 introduced any specific short-term effects on two important private rental sector outcomes: rent levels and property turnover. This seeks to complement previous reviews of neighborhood-level rental policy with additional evidence using a novel dataset on private rental sector listings, a unique causal identification strategy, and two separate estimation strategies.

Background: What are DLAs?

The discretionary licensing area (DLA) is a sub-city private rental sector regulatory tool intended to tackle specific urban social problems that are seen as relating to or otherwise influenced by issues in the housing market. The policy framework was established by the 2004 Housing Act, in which the Westminster government gave local authorities in England and Wales the power to declare selective licensing areas. The Act also introduced mandatory licensing for Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) and allowed for the creation of additional licensing schemes. The Act places requirements on how and why discretionary licensing policies can be enacted and who ultimately approves the creation of a DLA. The details of these requirements have changed over time (Wilson 2023). For our purposes, discretionary licensing policies can be enacted with the aim of resolving issues such as low housing demand (i.e. urban blight), anti-social behavior, low housing supply, or poor quality housing, but also can include areas of high migration. As such, DLAs must be specific, targeted neighborhood-level regulations that seek to achieve a specific policy outcome, such as increasing housing demand as necessary to reduce urban blight, reduction in anti-social behavior ordinances or general crime, improvement in housing conditions, or reducing (or limiting the growth of) overcrowding due to in-migration. Landlords operating within a designated DLA are expected to submit to property inspections when required, meet all licensing conditions—which are set locally in the light of the problem(s) being targeted—and pay a licence fee. Operating within a DLA without a valid licence is a criminal offence. The local authority is the enforcing body.

Further, DLAs are time-limited: they are designated for five years, with the possibility of renewal. Selective Licensing, which applies to all properties on the private rental market within a designated area, can operate alongside additional licensing schemes that target specific segments of the rental market. In many UK cities, additional licensing requirements can be applied to HMOs—dwellings where tenancies involve more than two people sharing a toilet, bathroom, or kitchen—that are not covered by mandatory HMO licensing; these are typically smaller properties. Additional licensing typically involves further documentation and/or inspection requirements for the property.

In Bristol selective and additional licensing requirements have been applied across the city at different times. As a neighborhood-level rental market regulation, two city wards (Eastville and St George West) have been designated as selective licensing areas (SLAs) from 2016-2021, but a very large portion of Bristol was covered with additional licensing regulation starting in 2019 and ending in 2024. This included most of the wards in central Bristol, as shown in Figure 1. In Bristol, selective licensing requirements are inclusive of additional requirements, meaning that the introduction of selective licensing includes all properties that would be captured in an additional licensing scheme. We denote this as selective+ for specificity, while additional licensing will be referred to as such. In Bristol, treatment under any DLA scheme occurs in three tranches; the first applying selective licensing to all private rental properties in two eastern wards, the second applying additional licensing across central Bristol, and the third applying selective licensing in two south Bristol wards—Bedminster and Brislington West—and extending additional licensing northward.

Implementation

So, what must be done if a property is regulated under selective or additional licensing designation? Typically, it requires the landlord to pay a fee of between £900 and £1500 pounds (depending on the configuration of the property and the licensing scheme), and formally record property quality and information on legally-mandated compliance, such as a gas safety certificate, an up-to-date energy performance certificate, and an electrical installation condition report. Together, these are intended to ensure that the property is of sufficient quality as to be let to tenants. Property inspections within DLAs are typically looking to identify “hazards” as defined by the Housing Health and Safety Rating System and encourage, or if necessary compel, landlords to remedy them. This is a risk-based system for identifying property defects, also introduced by the 2004 Housing Act.

Some landlords and advocacy groups argue that licensing schemes impose undue fiduciary and non-fiduciary costs on landlords. Landlords then pass these costs through to tenants, resulting in increased rent. Alternatively, individual landlords refrain from entering the private rental sector, ceding market participation to only well-resourced actors who are able to pay the licensing fees. This reduces the presence of buy-to-let activity in a licensed area, and also reduces the incentive to create new private rental properties.

These unintended effects of licensing schemes must be balanced against their intended outcomes. If these effects do exist and are severe, then we need to know about it. Alternatively, if these effects are not severe, then existing evidence suggests that these licensing schemes do work to improve their intended outcomes within the jurisdiction of the regulated area, with little negative externality on nearby areas. Therefore, investigating these potential unintended impacts of licensing schemes on the private rental market price levels and supply is important for understanding and assessing the use of DLAs as a policy instrument.

Methods and Data

In order to estimate these effects precisely, we use a novel dataset of scraped property listings from a private rental sector data provider, vendored through the Urban Big Data Centre at the University of Glasgow, UK. The data ostensibly provides information on all of the private rental properties listed in the UK from 2018 to 2023. We take a subset of this data focused on Bristol post codes, and filter the data for apparent duplicates, such as listings that are made for the same property over the same time period. Thus, this provides fairly solid data spanning the introduction of SLAs in 2019 and 2022, providing information on property characteristics, such as the number of bedrooms, bathrooms, and reception rooms available to rent with the listing, as well as user-contributed pictures, information on the letting agent (if applicable), full-text, short-text, and bullet-point descriptions of the listing. We take as outcomes the weekly rent charged and the duration the listing is live, and we use exogenous information about the property, such as the number of bedrooms, bathrooms, reception areas, etc. as predictors.

Occasionally, a listing’s characteristics will be modified during its lifetime. This might happen, for instance, if a one-bedroom property is listed as a two-bedroom property by mistake. These errors are rare, but we still only retain properties whose primary characteristics do not change during their listing. Alternatively, changes to a listing’s price can indicate that tenants are not expressing interest in the property at the initial price point. Fortunately, the data provider lists the sequence of price changes over the life of the listing (although we do not know when in the listing life the changes are made). From this, we can see that the general trend for price updates over the life of the listing is negative, suggesting landlords or agents are reducing the price in order to find a tenant willing to accept that price. Therefore, we take the last price on the listing as indicative of the clearing price.1 We take the duration the listing was live, from first post to removal from the platform, as an indication of market turnover. Since the measure increases as the turnover slows, we call this the staleness of the listing. The platform itself requires the removal of listings that have gone let-agreed, so we can be reasonably sure that the listing length corresponds to time-on-market for most properties, but, some clearly-stale listings stay on the platform for over a year. Thus, we anticipate this outcome to be less straightforward to model in this application, and take the results of this staleness analysis with a grain of salt.

Unfortunately for us, this timeline is also fundamentally confounded by the COVID-19 pandemic. While we can thus make indicative statements of the six-month period after the introduction of the first SLAs pre-COVID, we cannot make hard claims about the specific effect of the SLAs separate from the time over which they were implemented. In essence, this is true of any policy being analyzed, but in practice the COVID-19 pandemic and associated stay-at-home orders were exceptional impacts on life in the United Kingdom (and elsewhere) during the study period. Indeed, these effects also adjusted individuals’ likely tastes and preferences for short-term housing pushing people further out of the city center (Spell and Perry, n.d.).

In effect, this forces an identification strategy of three periods: (A) pre-SLA, (B) the immediate short-term impact of SLAs on the private rental sector in the nine months since first deployment, and the (C) long-run post-lockdown market structure. These periods are clearly evident in Figure 4, Figure 2, and Figure 3. While we can clearly see a reduction in supply across the treatment boundary in Figure 3, the later COVID-19 pandemic clearly suppresses supply further. However, listing geography is quite heterogeneous, as noted in Figure 6; where supply decreases (and thus price increases) is almost as important as that these changes occur. Hence, we need a more precise spatially-local identification strategy to differentiate these outcomes.

Therefore, when thinking about the identification of the effect of selective licensing areas on various rental market outcomes, like rent levels, rent growth, turnover, or volume, it is important to acknowledge a few things that can improve our ability to assign changes directly to the effect of SLAs. First, aggregate comparisons of rent levels or private rental sector size and turnover are likely to be hopelessly confounded by the wide-reaching changes induced by the COVID-19 pandemic, given the wide-ranging changes in life due to the stay-at-home orders. Therefore, this paper uses two different strategies in order to create a structured comparison between treated and untreated properties.

First, we will attempt a straightforward spatial difference in discontinuities specification for this data. At the DLA boundary, properties are most likely to be substitutes, while far outside (or inside) the DLA boundary, properties are unlikely to be substitutes—a city center property is never going to reasonably be compared to a property in a far-out commuter community. However, a standard difference in differences application would construct such a comparison. Therefore, we need to focus on the local effect close to the DLA boundary.

To do this, the SDID strategy calculates the discontinuity in outcome that exists at the DLA boundary pre-treatment and compares this to the boundary that exists at the DLA boundary after treatment. This acknowledges that listings are really only comparable directly near the boundary of the DLA. Imagine that the DLA ends up inflating rents through cost passthrough, as claimed by landlord interest groups. If this is the case, then properties near the boundary within the DLA should grow in rent faster than those outside the boundary. If the boundary starts showing that properties within the DLA are more expensive, then we expect the difference in discontinuities to be positive: the discontinuity between DLA and not-DLA should grow. In truth, we see the exact opposite; properties just inside of the DLA boundary start slightly cheaper and become much cheaper after a year of DLA implementation.

Second, we will use a spatial \(X\)-learner (Künzel et al. 2019) strategy to address any imbalance in the treated/untreaetd cohort at the boundary. This is a causal machine learning strategy whereby separate estimators are fit to the treated and untreated groups. Treatment effects are estimated as the difference between the treated model’s predictions and the untreated model’s predictions, weighted by the propensity of a property to enter the treatment group. This second propensity model corrects for potential sample imbalance, since observations just within the treated area may systematically differ from observations just outside of the treated area. Like typical doubly-robust estimation, the causal effect is identified when the treatment and control models are well fit or the propensity score model is well-fit. Further, the \(X\)-learner collapses to a simpler \(T\)-learner (i.e. two-model learner) if there is perfect separation between treatment and control models. And, it further collapses to an even simpler \(S\)-learner (i.e. single-model learner) if there is no heterogeneity in the treatment and control models. Given the intensely spatial nature of the rental market and the possibility of spatial heterogeneity in the rental market process, the \(X\)-learner is necessary for our case. In our specific empirical example, this \(X\)-learner will be composed of a local regression fit on data within the DLA, a local regression outside of the DLA, and a local logistic regression on data near the boundary. The causal effect is then estimated using the difference between the predicted outcomes for houses on the boundary, weighted by their propensity to be treated.

We expect the \(X\)-learner to work well in this case given the arguments above. And, for cross-sectional analysis, we expect such a model will work quite well. However, given rental pricing is notoriously sticky and experiences a unique ratcheting effect (Wang and Zhou 2000; Gallin and Verbrugge 2019), we also need to control for changes in time across the treatment introduction. For this model to adequately control for starting conditions, we use a unique matching procedure focused on creating a quartet of observations that form a structured comparison between the treated observation and its predecessor pre-treatment and another observation identical to the treated observation (a spatial substitute), which would never be treated. Conditioning on these predecessors, we this analysis shifts the identification strategy to a spatial difference in discontinuities analysis: we seek to identify whether there is a discontinuity at the treatment boundary in a model of the outcome controlling for the trend.

Still, simply comparing the differences between these matches’ differences over the policy boundary is only a partial story—the actual policy areas where DLAs are implemented are decidedly non-random. In some sense, it is impossible to compare one property in the center of Bristol to another at the periphery and assume that their rental dynamics will (or ought) to be the same. The dynamics of city-center properties will nearly always differ from city-edge properties, hence the importance of the spatial component of the identification strategy. Yet, all temporally-varying effects that matter in this study, such as the differential impact of COVID-19 pandemic and stay-at-home orders, affect properties on either side of the boundary equally. That is, despite the fact that COVID-19 may shift preferences for rental properties out of the city centre, this effect is irrelevant to properties immediately adjacent to the DLA boundary. Thus, creating good, well-balanced comparisons near the boundary is critical for identification of the causal effect of DLA introduction.

Finding Local Spatial Substitutes

We consider the use of treated local spatial substitutes, or nearby similar properties, to pre-treatment listings. These can be thought of as approximate matches, in the sense that one two-bed one-bathroom end of terrace might be judged as a substitute for a similar property in the same estate listed later. Indeed, matching locally to treated spatial substitutes is a useful technique to ensure that approximate comparisons can be made across the data, maximizing the use of the initial pre-treatment listings. Notably, this is quite different from simply picking later matched properties that are most similar on attributes—indeed, spatially-constraining the matches will invariably degrade any a-spatial measure of match quality if there are any non-local optimal matches. However, using local spatial substitutes in place of exact nonlocal matches ensures that substitutes have (nearly) the same set of unmeasured locational confounders as the target property for matching.

To clearly define the matching procedure, it helps to define a few different types of observations. First, a treated listing is one made in a DLA that was made during the treatment period. We distinguish pre-treatment listings made in a ward before the DLA came into effect, while a never-treated listing is one located in a ward where a DLA was never introduced. A substitute is a donor listing near (or colocated with) a target listing with identical characteristics. If substitutes are contemporaneous, they are live at the same time, such that a prospective tenant might actually have considered both properties. Thus, we make pairs of treated listings and untreated substitutes for geographic matches. Then, we find a listing made before the DLA came into effect, called a precedent. Then, we aim to construct a quartet of observations, all with identical characteristics, such that the treatment listing and its predecessor, the treatment listing and its substitute control, and the substitute control listing and its predecessor are close to one another.

This can be optimised in two ways. First, it helps to note that finding a precedent for a treated observation does not affect finding a substitute, since substitutes are outside the DLA and the pretreatment precedent is inside the DLA. Therefore, the treated-pretreatment matching can be optimised separately from any other decision. Second, the match quality for selecting a substitute for each treated observation must consider both the distance between the treated observation and its substitute and the substitute and its precedent. For a simple example, imagine we have two potential substitutes available for treated observation \(A\): substitute \(B\) is 250 meters away and substitute \(C\) is 300 meters away. If we choose substitute \(B\), we then must find a precedent for \(B\). If \(B\) has no nearby precedent, then we might instead prefer selecting substitute \(C\). Indeed, in the worst case, \(C\)’s predecessor \(C'\) is colocated with \(C\), so the total match distance from assigning \(C\) as \(A\)’s substitute is just the distance between \(A\) and \(C\), \(d(A,C)\). However, \(B\)’s only available precedent might be \(C'\), making the total match distance from assigning \(B\) as \(A\)’s substitute \(d(A,B) + d(B,C')\). Hence, once there are at least two substitutes, we must consider the choice of substitute and the substitute’s precedent at the same time in order to optimize the entire quartet. Simply optimizing each step in turn may lead to suboptimal outcomes. Finally, consider that while we might seek matches for all treated observations, we only really need to consider spatial substitutes near the boundary of the DLA for the purposes of the analysis. Thus, including all treated properties in the matching will likely degrade the performance of the matching procedure, as interior treated observations consume available untreated candidates for matching. Therefore, we will ensure that match-based estimates take into account the match distance for efficient estimation.

Identification Challenges

Finally, it is useful to discuss a few challenges to identification.

First, properties listed in 2018 and again after 2019 may not necessarily be typical properties for the private rental market. That is, if a property is re-let every year, it’s unlikely to reflect long-term stable tenancies that, while not common, are nonetheless present. Indeed, DPS estimates place the typical tenancy close to three years (Service 2025). Unfortunately, given the span of the data, we cannot significantly lengthen the study window to capture this effect. However, this does magnify the importance of the local spatial substitutes—since any one property let in 2018 may never recur in our data, we can leverage nearby similar properties as a proxy to understand what such a property would obtain if re-let on the private rental market at a given point in time. This is a secondary motivation for using spatial substitutes to define predecessors, if necessary.

Second, we make no specific assignation of whether the DLA causes changes in the housing market through the landlord or the tenant mechanism. To illustrate, renters might view the DLA as conferring extra protections (it does not necessarily do so) or obligations on the landlord to the tenant (similarly so). If they do, any premium for regulated properties might arise simply from renters preferring to live in licensed properties and, as such, live within a DLA. Alternatively, any supply or turnover changes may similarly arise from altered tenant behavior. A tenant on the margin such might attempt to extend their tenancy instead of finding new accommodation if they valued its status as a licensed property. On balance, this would result in higher local rents and slower local rental markets with fewer properties being let per unit time. Even if there is only an additional licensing scheme in a given DLA, this effect may occur as pressure on HMO supply, driving tenants into smaller less-affordable households with fewer co-tenants.

The supply-side story is quite different, but would have similar apparent empirical effects. Given that discretionary licensing compliance is required regardless of whether or not a tenancy turns over, it would not specifically incentivise landlords to retain (or turf out) tenants. However, landlords still might view obeying the terms of the DLA as an onerous extra cost and thus seek to exit the rental market, since there is both a price of applying for a license, certification processes to ensure minimum quality for rented accommodation, and (potentially) an inspection by the city council during the term of the license (typically five years). This combination of fiduciary and non-fiduciary costs could indeed depress landlord participation in the rental market on the margin, which would reduce supply. In turn, this mechanism then may increase rents charged and lower market turnover. This latter justification was decisively argued by community groups during the local consultations about DLA implementation, as well as at least one UK-wide landlord advocacy group.

In order to address questions about identifying the specific mechanism by which changes affect the market, we would need more precise information about the rental market, such as within-tenancy rent changes and links to house sales to confirm rental market exits. The latter is possible, but the former is unlikely without an officially-maintained private rental sector database.

Estimation

Both the SDIDc and X-learner identification strategies construct their causal effect estimates by comparing predictions between actual and counterfactual treatment statuses. This means we do not necessarily need to focus on a specific parameter estimate for the control variates. Indeed, this liberates us to use quite flexible local models. Thus, we use geographical random forests (Georganos et al. 2019) from the spml package (Martin Fleischmann et al. 2026) to construct locally-nonlinear models relating exogenous listing-specific predictors (like the number of bedrooms, bathrooms, reception areas, floors) to the outcomes under study. For the SDID models, we allow for outcomes in one model to be used as a predictor for the other outcome model as well, meaning that the model analyzing rent levels considers listing duration as a predictor, and the model analyzing staleness can consider the advertised rent as a predictor. The X-learner models, described below, use only characteristics fixed before treatment. Throughout, we use simple 5-fold crossvalidation to train the (local) random forests, and use the same approach to identify a scale parameter that governs the local model.

For the spatial difference in discontinuity model, we estimate one model for each treatment status (pre/post and in/out of DLA) and outcome. For the X-learner, we estimate two models for each condition and outcome (one for treatment and another for control), and one propensity model used for both. The first model is a predictive model of the outcome fit inside or outside of the treatment zone. The second is a predictive model of whether or not a property might be located inside or outside of the treatment zone given its characteristics.

For the SDIDc model, we compare the difference in predicted outcomes at the boundary pre-treatment to the difference in predicted in outcomes at the boundary post-treatment. So,

Therefore, pre-treatment control is unnecessary directly in the post-treatment models. However, the X-learner does need to account for pre-treatment differences. It does this by modelling the change in each outcome between a listing and its matched predecessor, rather than the outcome itself, so that persistent differences between properties inside and outside the DLA are differenced out, as in the SDID. Using the predecessor’s outcome as a predictor instead only partly removes these differences: rents are persistent, but not perfectly so, and in this data each pound of predecessor rent predicts only about 63 pence of current rent, which would leave part of the pre-existing premium inside the DLA in the estimated treatment effect. The X-learner’s outcome models therefore use only characteristics fixed before treatment: the number of bedrooms, reception rooms, and floors, whether the listing ended after the first COVID-19 lockdown, the month in which it ended, and the time elapsed since its matched predecessor, over which rent growth accrues.2 Then, we calculate predictions for each observation’s actual model—the model trained on data that matches the observation’s treatment status—and compare this to the prediction from that observation’s counterfactual model, trained on observations that have a different treatment status. Quartets in which either listing’s rent more than triples or falls by more than two thirds relative to its predecessor, or in which any rent exceeds £2,000 per week, are excluded from the X-learner, since these almost always reflect monthly rents recorded as weekly or mismatched properties; this removes about 4% of listings. Because treatment is almost perfectly determined by location, a geographically-local model of the propensity score cannot be estimated in most places. The X-learner’s propensity score is therefore estimated with a (non-spatial) random forest using the same pre-treatment characteristics, using out-of-bag predictions.

Results

In terms of describing the matching process and data characteristics, it’s useful to note a few subtotals. Around half (20,238) of the 42,838 listings are in treated areas, with the vast majority of potentially treated listings (16,198) occurring in the Bristol additional licensing area adopted from 2019 to 2024. Out of these listings in the central DLA, about half (7,637) occur after the introduction of the DLA, half again are within 1km of the boundary (4,581). Of these listings, a simple matching that minimizes the distance separating matched properties with identical characteristics manages 93% efficiency: 4,293 listings are fully matched. The procedure finds predecessors with identical characteristics let at least a year prior that minimize the total distance from treated and predecessor listings. Then, the procedure finds the optimal set of contemporaneous untreated substitutes (within 90 days), and then optimal substitute predecessors let at least a year prior. Because the matching is exact, no listing is used twice.

The locality of these matches still leaves something to be desired. Maps and match distance distributions are shown in Figure 5. While we might expect short match distances within the city, it’s not obvious why substitutes are drawn linking, say, listings in the southwest outskirts of Bristol (i.e. Long Ashton) out to dormitory towns (Clevedon, Nailsea); while these are indeed substitutes for certain kinds of tenants, they are not as hyper-local as one might hope. Longer-term temporal data may improve this, but the analysis is also fundamentally limited by the size of the rental market in Bristol.

Regardless, the covariate balance is exceptional for these quartets: distributions are shown in Figure 6, and confirm that the exogenous covariate match dimensions (beds & bathrooms) match perfectly and uncontrolled exogenous dimensions (reception count) are also undistinguishable among matches, while endogenous values (rent charged, listing time on market) differ between some quartet components. This indicates the matching has worked as intended: drawing a property at random, we couldn’t distinguish whether it was a treatment listing, a predecessor of a treatment listing, a substitute, or a predecessor of a substitute unless we looked at its outcome values. Parametric tests of this balance are shown in Table 2, which provides two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests across pairs of the four groups along five covariates in Figure 6, largely confirming the visual intuition.

In terms of the composition of the panel itself after constructing the quartets, we can see in figure Figure 7 that there is significant time-varying heterogeneity in both the listing totals their relative share of the private rental sector. One can see the relative peaks in supply over the winter months in 2019 and 2020, as well as the post-COVID dropoff in March of 2020. However, there are no immediately apparently changes to the listing totals, either compositionally or in total across the treatment boundary. One can also see quite a different pattern in Figure 8, where listing durations peak in the summer and decline into the winter. This effect is pronounced for the pretreatment areas within Bristol City Center, and is quite muted for the untreated areas. In addition, we see a slight peak in listing durations immediately after the introduction of DLAs in Bristol city centre, but it is unclear whether this is an effect of the policy.

Spatial Difference in Discontinuity

In terms of the spatial difference in discontinuity model, we can from Figure 9 see the models are passable at predicting the price across treatment boundaries, but the duration predictions are fairly poor. This comports with our expectations from first principles about what “staleness” represents in this data. Still, the price predictions are passable here, given the heterogeneity of the market and the relatively limited information used to make predictions.

The group means for the SDID specification are shown in Table 3, while the estimated treatment effects are shown in Figure 10, with significance assessment using wild/simple bootstraps. Each entry in Table 3 is the average difference between the predicted outcome for a listing from the model trained on its own side of the boundary and the prediction from the model trained on the other side. For listings inside the DLA (pretreat and treated), a positive value means that the inside model predicts a higher rent for the same property; for listings outside (presubstitute and substitute), a negative value means the same thing. The discontinuity at the boundary in each period is therefore the difference between the inside and outside rows, and the treatment effect is the change in this discontinuity: (treated − substitute) − (pretreat − presubstitute).

Before DLA introduction, models trained inside the DLA predicted higher rents than models trained outside it for the same properties near the boundary: the pre-treatment discontinuity is about £38 per week, and about 2 days for listing duration. This initial discontinuity is a straightforward comparison of the local rents near the boundary pre-treatment. After the DLA was introduced, models trained inside the DLA still predicted higher rents, but by less: the post-treatment discontinuity is about £23. The change in the discontinuity is therefore about −£15 per week (bottom row, right pane of Figure 10): the premium for properties just inside the boundary narrowed after the DLA came into force. Over the entire regulated area (top row, right pane), the change is negligible (about £1 per week), but this comparison includes very central properties for which outlying rentals are not really substitutes. For listing duration, the changes are small: about 2.5 days overall and 3.6 days close to the boundary, the latter not distinguishable from zero.

\(X\)-learner Results

The \(X\)-learner identification strategy points in the same direction. In this case, we fit local models of the change in each outcome since the quartet predecessor, inside of and outside of the DLA. We then calculate the difference between the actual model and counterfactual model at the boundary, and calculate the propensity-weighted average3 of the estimated individual treatment effects. Considering model adequacy in Figure 11, changes in both outcomes are poorly predicted by property characteristics alone. The predictions are weakly correlated with the observed changes (\(r\) of about 0.21 to 0.28 for rent and 0.03 to 0.17 for listing duration), but they vary more than so weak a relationship warrants, so their out-of-sample \(R^2\) is below zero: they are no more accurate than predicting the average change for every listing.

Finally, we consider the causal effect estimates in Figure 12 and Table 4. Across all quartets, rents in regulated areas grew slightly less than outside them: the treatment effect is about −£2.30 per week, even after taking into account starting rent levels and price fluctuations due to COVID-19. This effect is distinguishable from zero in both the bootstrap and the propensity-shuffled bootstrap.4 Because most quartets pair a treated listing with a distant substitute, Table 5 also weights quartets by a triangular kernel in the distance between the treated listing and its substitute, mirroring the SDID’s weighting by distance to the boundary. The estimate is more negative when the comparison is more local: about −£4.60 per week with a 3 km bandwidth, −£6.10 with 2 km, and −£5.40 (95% interval −£10.60 to −£0.60) with 1 km. For clearing speed, listings within the DLA stay live about 1.6 days less on average, which is distinguishable from zero; the distance-weighted estimates are similar, about 1.8 to 2.6 days less, although the 1 km estimate is not distinguishable from zero. This is consistent with the small SDID duration estimate and suggests the DLA had no meaningful impact on how quickly properties were let.

Comparing the estimates

The SDID and X-learner estimates differ in magnitude, in part because they compare different listings. The SDID compares listings on either side of the boundary directly, while most X-learner quartets pair a treated listing with a substitute several kilometres away (median 3.7 km; only 4% within 1 km). Figure 13 shows both estimates as their comparisons are restricted to listings closer to the boundary. For the SDID, the boundary discontinuity in each group is estimated by a local-linear regression on signed distance to the boundary with a triangular kernel, across bandwidths from 100 m to 3 km; for the X-learner, quartets are weighted by a triangular kernel in the distance between the treated listing and its substitute, with the same bandwidths. The SDID estimate is negative at every bandwidth from 200 m, between about −£15 and −£34 per week; at a 1 km bandwidth it is −£28 (95% bootstrap interval −£39 to −£14). The X-learner estimate is about −£5 per week (−£11 to −£1) at a 1 km bandwidth and about −£6 between 1.1 and 2 km; at 900 m and below it is not distinguishable from zero. The two estimates agree in sign, but from 1 km outward the SDID estimate is three to five times larger, and their intervals overlap only at 400 m and between 1.4 and 1.6 km. Neither estimator finds a meaningful effect on listing duration near the boundary. Restricted to local comparisons, both strategies therefore indicate that the rent premium for properties just inside the DLA narrowed after its introduction.

Discussion and Conclusion

Discretionary licensing is an important tool for local government in regulating the private rental sector in England and Wales. The use of these policies must generally target concerns about poor housing quality, urban market failure, or anti-social behavior, but some argue that the use of selective and additional licensing authority introduces unnecessary additional costs that get passed off onto tenants through higher rents. In addition, these policies have been suggested to drive landlords out of the rental market.

The analysis here provides little evidence that the introduction of discretionary licensing policies in central Bristol wards starting in 2019 reduced supply or raised rents in the short run. Before the DLA, properties just inside its boundary commanded a rent premium over comparable properties just outside; after its introduction, this premium narrowed, by about £15 to £30 per week in the spatial difference in discontinuity and by about £5 per week for closely-matched quartets in the X-learner. Rental market clearing shows no meaningful change: both estimates of the DLA’s effect on listing staleness near the boundary are small and not distinguishable from zero. This does not support the concern that licensing costs are passed through to tenants as higher rents, at least over this period. If licensing improved quality, or if tenants treated a licence as a signal of quality, rents inside the DLA would be expected to rise relative to those outside; that they did not suggests that compliance costs were largely absorbed by landlords, or that licensing curbed rents at the top of the local market. Despite controls and data selection strategies to avoid later COVID-19 effects on housing preferences, the analysis cannot rule out that the narrowing reflects changes in demand for central locations over 2018–2021 that happened to coincide with the DLA’s introduction.

Identifying these short-run changes is important for building longer-term understanding of the efficacy of these minimum standards-type rental regulations. Indeed, while the impact of price controls on housing quality are well understood for rent control, the effects of these kinds of minimum standard or inspection-type licensing strategies are not as well understood. Thus, the next step is to investigate whether this evidence of a narrowing rent premium within DLA boundaries, with no corresponding change in clearing speed, is replicated elsewhere.

  1. Note that we do not argue this is actually the rent charged to tenants. Many tenants inquiring about rental listings in this period may have engaged in post-listing bidding competitions with other tenants, driving the final rent charged higher than the public market clearing price. Alternatively, the listing’s original post date is visible on the platform, so some savvy tenants may choose to under-bid the public price on a particularly stale listing.↩︎

  2. We acknowledge this is slightly imperfect, since any two quartets may have different delays between current and predecessor listings; if one listing in 2020 might be matched to a predecessor in 2018, while a different listing in 2022 might also be matched to a predecessor in 2018. While the rate of rent growth may be constant, the two will experience quite a different relationship between previous and current rent. In practice these delays are short and similar on both sides of the boundary: the median gap is 1.5 years for treated listings (interquartile range 1.1–1.9) and 1.3 years for substitutes (1.0–1.7). Treated listings are thus about two months further from their predecessors on average, which, if anything, would bias the rent estimate upwards; the X-learner therefore includes this interval as a predictor.↩︎

  3. The propensity model simply scores whether or not an individual listing is likely to enter the treatment set. This is useful when there is heterogeneity in the treated and untreated population—for example, very large properties may exist among untreated listings↩︎

  4. Variability in these plots is likely understated, since the bootstrap does not re-estimate the underlying models.↩︎
